studies.Reference: Blood magnesium, and the interaction with calcium, on the risk of high-grade prostate cancer.
studies.Authors: Dai Q, Motley SS, Smith JA, Concepcion R, Barocas D, Byerly S, Fowke JH
studies.direction_imputation_reason: Comparison direction was not explicit; the protocol assumes high versus low exposure.
studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: Serum concentration of magnesium and calcium were determined by standard analytic method on the Beckman DXC 800 chemistry analyzer provided by the Vanderbilt Pathology Laboratory Services with an intra-assay coefficient of variation of 2.0.

sample_size.excerpt: In this biomarker sub-study of the Nashville Men's Health Study (NMHS), we included 494 NMHS participants, consisting of 98 high-grade (Gleason≥7) and 100 low-grade cancer cases, 133 prostate intraepithelial neoplasia (PIN) cases, and 163 controls without cancer or PIN at biopsy.
sample_size.location: Methods, Data Analysis, paragraph 1; total_n derived from reported group counts 98 + 163 = 261

effect_size.excerpt: Elevated Mg was significantly associated with a lower risk of high-grade prostate cancer (OR = 0.26 (0.09, 0.85)).

p_value.excerpt: Serum Mg levels were significantly lower, while the Ca/Mg ratio was significantly higher, among high-grade cases vs. controls (p = 0.04, p = 0.01, respectively).

design.excerpt: In this biomarker sub-study of the Nashville Men's Health Study (NMHS), we included 494 NMHS participants, consisting of 98 high-grade (Gleason≥7) and 100 low-grade cancer cases, 133 prostate intraepithelial neoplasia (PIN) cases, and 163 controls without cancer or PIN at biopsy.

timing.excerpt: Blood was collected prior to diagnosis and treatment, and body size measures were ascertained by trained staff.

continent.excerpt: Men scheduled for a diagnostic prostate biopsy between 2002 and 2008 at a Vanderbilt University Medical Center (Nashville, TN), the Tennessee Valley Veteran's Administration Hospital (Nashville, TN), or a large private urology practice in Nashville, were approached for recruitment.

headline.funnel_interpretation: Egger’s test is generally not recommended when fewer than 10 studies are available.
headline.results_interpretation: The pooled analysis of 3 studies yielded an effect size of 1.05 (95% CI: 0.88–1.25), indicating no statistically significant association between magnesium and prostate cancer. Although the point estimate suggests a potential positive relationship, the confidence interval includes the null. These findings were accompanied by substantial heterogeneity (I² = 69.61%), reflecting considerable variability across studies.
